title: Step Inside the Studios of 20 Contemporary Black Artists in 'Another View'
description: One of the most intimate windows into an artist’s practice is their studio. While some creatives thrive on methodical organization and tidiness, o
body:
One of the most intimate windows into an artist’s practice is their studio. While some creatives thrive on methodical organization and tidiness, others reach their flow state amid a cluttered chaos where dozens of ideas unfold at once. Whether at one end of this spectrum or somewhere in the middle, these spaces offer unique perspectives on both the artist and the masterpieces that emerge from their confines.
Forthcoming from Phaidon, Another View: The Vibrant World of Contemporary Black Artists invites readers into 20 distinctive studios. Celebrating some of the most prominent artists working today—such as Nick Cave, Nina Chanel Abney, Hank Willis Thomas, Carrie Mae Weems, Kerry James Marshall, and many more—the seminal volume highlights a range of behind-the-scenes material.
Hank Willis Thomas, Brooklyn 
The introduction to Another View was written by lauded literary critic, filmmaker, and professor Henry Louis Gates, Jr. who “explores the historical precedents and critical context that led to the exciting current moment of Black contemporary art in America,” writes Phaidon. Across nearly 200 pages, the book includes 150 never-before-seen photographs, exclusive interviews, and profiles.
Another View: The Vibrant World of Contemporary Black Artists is slated for release on October 28. Pre-order your copy in the Colossal Shop.

title: Across Two Exhibitions, Jaume Plensa's Monumental Sculptures Unite Scale and Material
description: Measuring 28 feet wide and seven feet tall, two monumental wooden relief sculptures anchor Beyond Silence, a new exhibition at GRAY Chicago featur
body:
Measuring 28 feet wide and seven feet tall, two monumental wooden relief sculptures anchor Beyond Silence, a new exhibition at GRAY Chicago featuring works by Catalan artist and sculptor Jaume Plensa.
The broad works—titled “Julia” and “Maria”—were created as part of the artist’s recent series, Beyond Silence, which shares a name with the show. The two paneled pieces transform the gallery’s open exhibition space with their rigid angles, creating a structured rhythm to complement the subdued contours of the faces they depict. As a result, a conversation arises between Plensa’s signature overarching motifs, such as the human figure, use of architectural materials, and the perception of space.
“Maria” (2026). Cast iron and granite stone, 85 3⁄8 × 62 7⁄8 × 109 3⁄8 inches
Surrounding these wooden reliefs, viewers encounter dramatically elongated faces stretching seven feet high. The impressive portraits are part of Plensa’s Clouds series, in which the artist pairs cast iron—a material often associated with commercialism and industry—with the suavity of granite stone, “producing an unexpected sense of suspension and weightlessness,” the gallery says. 
Like many of Plensa’s works, the large faces stand with their eyes closed, allowing viewers to experience each monumental figure intimately. These impressive pieces evoke a quiet stillness and offer a unique space for introspection, meditation, and a sense of intimacy through shared humanity. 
Beyond Silence marks the artist’s tenth solo exhibition with GRAY, and coincides with Remote, Serene, Ethereal opening next week at the gallery’s New York location. Both exhibitions are on view through December 19. And if you’re in Chicago, you can always find Plensa’s iconic work, Crown Fountain, at Millennium Park. Find more from the artist on Instagram.
“Twilight III” (2025). Bronze, 20 3⁄4 × 8 5⁄8 × 8 1⁄4 inches. Edition of 7
“Silent Maria” (2025). Painted bronze, 71 5⁄8 × 27 1⁄8 × 35 3⁄8 inches. Edition of 5
“Beyond Silence (Julia)” (2026). Wood and steel, 85 3⁄8 × 339 1⁄4 × 41 1⁄4 inches
“Irmaleni” (2026). Cast iron and granite stone, 85 3⁄4 × 68 1⁄2 × 110 1⁄8 inches
“Twilight II” (2025). Bronze, 22 3⁄4 × 7 3⁄8 × 7 3⁄8 inches. Edition of 7

“Twilight VI” (2025). Bronze, 20 3⁄8 × 9 × 12 1⁄8 inches. Edition of 7

title: Buffalo Puppet Procession Traces Native History Through NYC’s Streets
description:
News
                “Return of the Buffalo: Tatanka Owe Akupi” pays homage to 38 Dakota men executed by President Abraham Linco
body:
News
                “Return of the Buffalo: Tatanka Owe Akupi” pays homage to 38 Dakota men executed by President Abraham Lincoln in Mankato, Minnesota, in 1862.
            
                
                                
                            
                
                
                    Anna Lee
                    September 18, 2026
                            — 3 min read
                    
                
            
                
        
            The buffalo procession began next to Bowling Green Park, stopping briefly in front of the National Museum of the American Indian. (photo Anna Lee/Hyperallergic) 
    
        
            A herd of 40 life-sized buffalo puppets migrated through Lower Manhattan today, September 18, plodding through Bowling Green, Federal Hall, the World Trade Center, Chinatown, and several other historical sites along their trail. On the second and final leg of its procession, Return of the Buffalo: Tatanka Owe Akupi (Lakota for "buffalo trail home") will also hit downtown Brooklyn tomorrow, September 19.Theater writer and director Amir Nizar Zuabi created the project with descendants of the Lenape, the original Indigenous inhabitants of New York, and Lakota elders, whose deeply sacred relationship with the mammal dates back thousands of years. “We just followed the elders’ lead in who they wanted involved, what they wanted to be said, really letting them shape the conceptual backbone of the work,” JJ Lind (Cherokee-Shawnee), the artistic director for the performance group Immediate Medium, told Hyperallergic.Buffalo make their way up Broadway Street (photo Anna Lee/Hyperallergic) “We’d bring community members in to provide feedback on the activities that happen along the route,” he added. At nine historic sites throughout Manhattan, such as Broad Street Plaza and Zuccotti Park, concurrent performances from the Native dance troupes, gospel choirs, and Lenape youth created a lively backdrop. From the rampant slaughter of buffalo in the 19th century to the species' recovery led by Native activists and conservationists, the procession traces the buffalo’s complex history in the United States.

title: NYC’s Shelter Population Speaks Out in Public Art Project
description:
Feature
                Alex Strada’s “Public Address” brings handwritten testimonies from over 400 unhoused New Yorkers and she
body:
Feature
                Alex Strada’s “Public Address” brings handwritten testimonies from over 400 unhoused New Yorkers and shelter staff to a dozen locations across the Bronx.
            
                
                                
                            
                
                
                    Anna Lee
                    September 18, 2026
                            — 4 min read
                    
                
            
                
        
            Cutout signs from staff workers or residents of NYC homeless shelters attached to a park fence as part of Alex Strada's Public Address (2025–) (all images courtesy the artist)
    
        
            Alex Strada’s Public Address opened in the Bronx on Monday, September 14, bringing handwritten testimonies from over 400 New York shelter residents and frontline staff to a dozen locations across the borough.Using log entries from workshops held across New York City shelters, Strada, public artist-in-residence with the NYC Department of Homeless Services and Department of Cultural Affairs since 2022, translated these messages onto aluminum signs from the Department of Transportation. Visible on street corners, parks, and other high-traffic areas, the long-term installation debuted in Manhattan in October 2025 and will have appeared in all five boroughs by March 2027."My hope for this project is that it functions as a jumping off point to work towards more just realities that are not mired in stereotype or misperception, or in the acceptance of homelessness as an unavoidable byproduct of New York City life,” Strada told Hyperallergic. Log entry from 2024, attached to a metal postThe project includes depictions of an Ecuadorian mother fleeing to New York with her two daughters, an assemblage of multicolored hearts, and intimate letters detailing experiences with homelessness. Bikes, houses, and faraway stretches of land convey privileges often taken for granted, and letters touch on lesser-known aspects of homelessness: the impossible prospect of finding housing as an undocumented immigrant, balancing high school without shelter, and the unforeseen circumstances that bring about eviction at a moment's notice.

title: No One Is Accountable in Taryn Simon’s Detective Story
description:
Art Review
                In her ambitious exhibition at the Guggenheim Museum, injustice seems purely systemic, not the result
body:
Art Review
                In her ambitious exhibition at the Guggenheim Museum, injustice seems purely systemic, not the result of individuals behaving badly. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Taryn Simon's "The Windows Exploded" series at the Guggenheim Museum in New York (all photos Aruna D'Souza/Hyperallergic)
    
        
            Taryn Simon’s ambitious show at the Guggenheim Museum, Father Country I Do Love You, begins with two text panels. One recounts a story told to her by her father, of an intelligence officer he met in Bangkok who died under mysterious circumstances — either eaten by a tiger, or kidnapped by the Chinese. It goes on to talk about her father’s penchant for taping his prized photos in plexiglass box frames. “Each came with a dramatic tale — delivering suitcases of cash to generals in Cambodia, yakuza threatening to break his arm in a door, having tea with his kidnappers in Lebanon, and starting the Thai stock exchange. I never got the full story,” reads the text.The second panel features Simon’s own terse account of meeting a retired FBI agent a decade ago and listening to his stories, meted out via phone calls, text messages, and meetings. He would become the main character of this sprawling show, his recollections offering impetus for her painstaking research. These introductory texts are set against teak paneling — a replica of a replica of the living room of the Bangkok spy that Simon helped her father build in their own family home when she was a child. Introductory text panels in ather Father Country I Do Love YouVia hundreds, maybe thousands, of photographs, as well as sculptures, video, and an exhibition design that suggests that replica living room with brightly-colored walls and heavy drapery, this exhibition purports to present information that might sound like conspiracy theories but are in fact facts. It connects stories and people and historical events and bureaucratic structures in ways that are both improbable and utterly realistic. But by prefacing it with her father’s tales which she could never confirm (“I never got the full story”), Simon keeps doubt, always, in play.The FBI agent’s work put him in the orbit of some of the most consequential events of his lifetime: the explosion of TWA Flight 800 in 1996 (he was one of many agents who had to analyze the remnants), the 9/11 attacks on the Pentagon (he was assigned to sift debris), al-Qaeda’s bombing of the United States embassy in Nairobi in 1998 (he was deployed there along with 900 other agents), the arrest of DC Mayor Marion Barry  on drug charges in 1990 (he babysat the children of the model sent to entrap him), Bill Clinton’s impeachment (he set up the evidence room), and more.

title: The Titillating Tale of Damien Hirst’s Gay Hole
description:
Performance
                An infectious play by Sleth explores infatuation and fame through an imagined relationship between H
body:
Performance
                An infectious play by Sleth explores infatuation and fame through an imagined relationship between Hirst and his gay lover, a younger artist whose paintings consist of holes on the ground.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Playwright Sleth as Shape in The Wreck of the Unbelievable (all photos Hrag Vartanian/Hyperallergic)
    
        
            The Wreck of the Unbelievable is a strangely infectious, if uneven, little play about obsession that takes on the fantastical premise in which renowned artist Damien Hirst is dead and is survived by a gay lover named Shape (smartly played by playwright Sleth), who greets theatergoers sprawled, ass up, on a disheveled mattress reminiscent of Tracey Emin’s “My Bed” (1998). The production makes it clear that Hirst is very much alive and straight, to the best of our knowledge, but the idea makes for a weird wormhole into the nature of infatuation and the costs of being an artist who craves the good stuff — fame and fortune.The off-off-Broadway play runs over 80 minutes, though it could easily clip 15 to tighten the storyline. The seemingly hungover artist is greeted by an old party friend named Mara who has since become an assistant curator at the Guggenheim Museum. Shape’s hardly impressed and jokes that it’s not exactly the Whitney Museum or MoMA. The plot focuses on his friend’s need to extract some seedy details of this secret affair for a rushed Hirst retrospective she's organizing at the museum. What was the YBA star really like, she asks? Hung, apparently — at least in this theatrical reimagining.What greeted theater goers as they filed into their seatsThe set design and direction are tight, with some poetic moments, like when Shape and Mara revisit their bohemian — or were they hipster? — yesteryears. A puff of smoke lingers above the performers like a Surrealist flourish to denote memory. In another flash, UV light floods the stage to reveal an eerie scene reminiscent of Sandy Skoglund’s haunting photographs.

title: The Cathedral of Joy
description:
Weekly Newsletter
								One-on-one with Alfredo Jaar, Damien Hirst’s secret life, Anish Kapoor's optical trickery, and another BS "most
body:
Weekly Newsletter
								One-on-one with Alfredo Jaar, Damien Hirst’s secret life, Anish Kapoor's optical trickery, and another BS "most influential" list.  
						
								
																
														
								
						
		
	  		    
        
    
		
				
						At a cafe named Anti Cafe — though it looks like any other cafe — a man is writing dozens of cards by hand, sealing them inside pretty little envelopes, and stacking them in a pile on the table. After half an hour of observing him from the next table, I finally ask, “Are those wedding invitations?” “Nope,” he replies.“Birthday party invitations?”“Nope.”“So what are they for, if you don’t mind me asking?”“Just letters to my friends to show them how much I appreciate them,” he discloses with an air of self-satisfaction. “Oh, that’s so beautiful,” I say with my hand on my heart, feeling sincerely touched. But as I leave the cafe, I begin wondering if that guy is okay. Down in the subway station, I see another young man using a Sharpie pen to make meticulous drawings of the Manhattan grid on a large piece of cardboard. Avenue by avenue, street by street, the lines in his map are perfectly straight without the use of a ruler. I see him doing the same thing on the same subway bench the next day and admire his dedication. On the third day, it dawns on me that this young artist lives in the subway. At night, I see a group of grinning people walking around with grabbers, searching for litter on the sidewalk. “We’re just helping clean up the neighborhood,” one of them tells me. “Oh, that’s so nice of you,” I say, feeling genuinely impressed. But then I notice that everyone is suspiciously good-looking and that there’s barely any litter to pick up. It appears that the members of this “trash club” are here to pick up more than just trash.  A flock of birds in the sky makes the shape of a middle finger, reminding me it’s migration season. At the pierogi place, not a single soul is Polish. Global Wealth Clothing sells garments to the poor. The Cathedral of Joy is in a miserable spot. A place called The Community is empty of people. And on one of the windows of a shiny new building, a sign reads in big letters: "Warning: rat infestation. Tenants on rent strike."—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chiefPS—If you’re in New York on September 30, come meet me at the International Studio & Curatorial Program, where we’ll talk to resident artists and enjoy some refreshments. 

	
		
		Alfredo Jaar Is Still Trying to Change the World
		
	
	
		In April of 1987, when Reaganism was running amok and Henry Kissinger was fiddling with world affairs like a puppet master from hell, a relatively unknown 31-year-old Chilean artist named Alfredo Jaar staged his billboard installation A Logo for America smack dab in the heart of Times Square. It instantly became one of the most discussed works of political art in the contemporary canon. 

Appearing between ads for tomato sauce and a Mexican restaurant, the 42-second LED animation bewildered New Yorkers with the message “This Is Not America” superimposed on a map of the United States, followed by an image of the US flag with the text, “This Is Not America’s Flag.” Next, the “R” in America shifted into a dancing map of South, Central, and North America. | Hakim Bishara
